prompt: `mistake.run()` printed `on main`. Why was no new thread involved?
hint: Only one method creates the thread.

choices.text: Threads named by default run on `main`
choices.why: `worker` had the default name and ran on `Thread-0`.
It had never started.

choices.text: The JVM ran it on `main` to save a thread, an optimisation it makes for short tasks
choices.why: The JVM makes no such choice; the call did exactly what it says.

choices.text: `run` is an ordinary call; only `start` creates a thread
choices.why: Right.
Threads are never merged.

choices.text: Stops `worker` if it is still running
choices.why: Nothing stops a thread from outside.
`start` does that.
Right.

prompt: `Thread.of___().name("invoice-", 1)` builds operating-system threads named `invoice-1`, `invoice-2` and so on.
Match each moment of `States.java` with the state it printed.
What does `sleeper.interrupt()` do to a thread that is sleeping?

choices.why: Java has no safe way to kill a thread.

choices.text: Nothing, until the sleep is over
choices.why: It woke after 200 ms, not five seconds.
Right, and the thread decides what to do.

choices.text: Restarts its `run` method from the top
choices.why: Nothing restarts a thread.

prompt: A method catches `InterruptedException`, cannot stop at once, and does nothing else. What is wrong?

choices.text: The exception should have been printed
choices.why: Printing does not tell the code above that a stop was requested.
It is checked; catching it is normal, ignoring it is the problem.

choices.text: The flag was cleared, so nobody above sees the request
choices.why: Right: call `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` to restore it.

choices.text: The thread is now `TERMINATED` and cannot continue
choices.why: It continues running; that is the trouble.

prompt: A program hangs. What does the lesson suggest reading first?

choices.why: A hang is threads waiting, which the dump shows.
Right.
The question is about your threads, not the class.
Memory does not say what a thread is waiting for.

prompt: How long did starting 10,000 platform threads take in `Cost.java`, in seconds, to one decimal place?
`Threads:` rose by about one per `start()`. What does that show?

choices.text: The JVM counts its own Java objects there
choices.why: It is the operating system's count, read from `/proc`.
Right: one for one.

choices.text: Threads are created lazily, when they first run
choices.why: They exist as soon as `start` returns.

choices.text: The machine has that many processors
choices.why: It has four.

prompt: Each thread reserves a megabyte of stack, yet resident memory grew by tens of kilobytes per thread. Why?

choices.text: Sleeping threads give their stack back to the JVM until they wake
choices.why: A sleeping thread keeps its stack.
The default is a megabyte.

choices.text: Most of the reservation is never touched
choices.why: Right, and it still counts against the process's limits.

choices.text: The garbage collector freed the stacks while they slept
choices.why: Thread stacks are not collected while the thread lives.

prompt: `worker-a` threw `ArithmeticException` and nobody caught it. What did `main` do?

choices.why: Nothing restarts a thread.
Right: the silent failure.
The exception ended `worker-a` only.
`join` returns normally; it reports nothing about how the thread ended.

prompt: Which of these give a failing thread a way to report its death? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: No: that decides whether the JVM waits for it.
Yes.

choices.text: Running it as a task in an executor, lesson 16
choices.why: Yes: the result carries the exception.
Yes.

prompt: Why did the daemon's line never appear?
hint: Who does the JVM wait for?

choices.text: The JVM exited when `main` ended, killing it
choices.why: Right: daemons are not waited for.

choices.text: It threw an exception nobody saw
choices.why: No trace was printed.

choices.text: `sleep` is not allowed in a daemon
choices.why: It is allowed.
They can; this one did not live long enough.

prompt: Put `sleeper`'s states in the order `States.java` printed them.
A server starts a platform thread per request, and requests mostly wait for a database. What limits how many it can serve at once?

choices.why: The threads mostly wait; processors are not the limit.
It changes the reservation per thread, not the cost of a thread per request.

choices.text: The number of platform threads it keeps alive
choices.why: Right: a few thousand, however little each does.

choices.text: The size of each request's body, which every thread must hold in memory at once
choices.why: The cost described is per thread, not per byte of request.
